items.claim: Every byte-checkable claim in this reading holds: the letter run, the mark and paseq disclosures, the ketiv/qere disclosure, the two formula digits and the refrain form all verify against the pointed text, and the third-person framing with one disclosed first-person plea at the close matches the forms.
items.evidence: Letters alef through tet stand at Lam.1.1-Lam.1.9 in the standard sequence of this poem, one letter per verse, exactly as disclosed. The opening cry אֵיכָ֣ה (oshb:Lam.1.1, byte tier) is verse-initial, and verse-initial placement of that token is attested in 3 verses book-wide (sweep: 3 verses, verse-initial only: Lam.1.1, Lam.2.1, Lam.4.1; the token also stands non-initially in 1 further verse, sweep: 4 verses for the token anywhere) - the cited digit names the verse-initial object, not the token census. The daughter-of-Zion phrase is a two-token test and stands in 8 verses book-wide (sweep: 8 verses, 8 token occurrences), so the 'seven further' arithmetic is right; the ketiv/qere note at Lam.1.6 is disclosed, which matters here because the note sits on that very phrase. Marks: SAMEKH at all nine verses, single-witness, none conflated with PE; one paseq segment at Lam.1.1, cited as a bare count. The contiguous refrain אֵ֥ין מְנַחֵ֖ם לָ֑הּ (oshb:Lam.1.9, byte tier; there is no one to comfort her) is attested in 3 verses (sweep: 3 verses for the contiguous two-token form: Lam.1.9, Lam.1.17, Lam.1.21), correctly distinguished from the wider comfort-word family attested in 5 verses of this poem (sweep: 5 verses) - the contiguous form is what is counted, and it is named. The 'otherwise third-person' description holds: a complete scan of Lam.1.1-Lam.1.8 returns no second-person and no first-person-singular form; the plea that follows the refrain inside Lam.1.9 is רְאֵ֤ה יְהוָה֙ אֶת עָנְיִ֔י (oshb:Lam.1.9, byte tier), an imperative plus vocative plus a first-person-singular noun, and the byte order inside the verse is refrain first, plea second, exactly as the reading sequences it. All five renderings quoted from the translation are verbatim in the staged text. No declared false-positive disposition falls on any verse of this span, so none is confirmed or refuted here. One presentational weakness, not a defect: the closing sentence points forward to a neighbouring interjection without anchoring it to its verse.

items.claim: The reading's discriminating ground - that person marking stays third-person until the plea at the end of Lam.1.11 - is contradicted by Lam.1.10, which addresses the deity in the second person, and the reading offers no Hebrew form anywhere to test the claim.
items.evidence: Lam.1.10 carries אֲשֶׁ֣ר צִוִּ֔יתָה (oshb:Lam.1.10, byte tier) - a second-person perfect - and בַקָּהָ֖ל לָֽךְ (oshb:Lam.1.10, byte tier), a second-person pronoun; the addressee is the deity, and both stand before the closing plea of Lam.1.11. The rendering the reading itself quotes carries the same datum: “concerning whom you commanded that they should not enter into your assembly.” web:Lam.1.10 - so the counter-evidence is quoted while the opposite is asserted, and the rejected alternative rests on the same false premise. This is a person and form claim argued with zero quoted Hebrew: the reading contains no Hebrew run at all, so nothing in it is testable at byte tier on its own terms. Weighed from both sides of the front seam, the address feature also straddles it: Lam.1.9 closes with רְאֵ֤ה יְהוָה֙ אֶת עָנְיִ֔י (oshb:Lam.1.9, byte tier), the same imperative-plus-vocative address to the deity, so second-person address is present on both sides of the seam and in the span's own first verse - undisclosed. What holds: letters yod and kaf are correct; the mark disclosure is complete and correctly typed at the front-seam neighbour and both interior verses; the ketiv/qere note at Lam.1.11 is disclosed; both translation renderings are verbatim.

items.claim: The reading asserts one continuous first-person city voice across Lam.1.12-Lam.1.17, but the final verse of the span carries no first-person form at all and speaks of the city in the third person, so the unit label, the refrain-close argument and the high confidence are not carried by the bytes.
items.evidence: Lam.1.12 through Lam.1.16 carry first-person-singular marking in every verse - כְּמַכְאֹבִ֔י (oshb:Lam.1.12, byte tier), הֱשִׁיבַ֣נִי (oshb:Lam.1.13, byte tier), פְּשָׁעַ֜י (oshb:Lam.1.14, byte tier), בְּקִרְבִּ֔י (oshb:Lam.1.15, byte tier), נַפְשִׁ֑י (oshb:Lam.1.16, byte tier). Lam.1.17 carries none: a complete token scan of that verse returns zero first-person-singular forms, and the verse runs third-person feminine throughout - פֵּֽרְשָׂ֨ה צִיּ֜וֹן בְּיָדֶ֗יהָ (oshb:Lam.1.17, byte tier), אֵ֤ין מְנַחֵם֙ לָ֔הּ (oshb:Lam.1.17, byte tier), הָיְתָ֧ה יְרוּשָׁלִַ֛ם (oshb:Lam.1.17, byte tier). The refrain used to close the unit therefore stands inside a narrator verse, not inside the city's speech, and its suffix is the third-person feminine one - the same form as at the first site and not the first-person form at the third site, a contrast the reading elsewhere shows it had available. Weighing both sides of the back seam as a refrain-side diagnosis requires: the last first-person verse of the span is Lam.1.16, and first-person marking resumes immediately at Lam.1.18 with מָרִ֑יתִי (oshb:Lam.1.18, byte tier; this verse carries a ketiv/qere note, disclosed here because a form is spliced from it) - so a seam at Lam.1.16 with Lam.1.17 as a third-person bridge is at least as well supported by the forms as the seam taken, and it is not weighed. A high-confidence label on a span whose voice description fails at its last verse is uncalibrated; the honest posture is a held medium_low with the bridge question named. What holds: the letters lamed, mem, nun, samekh, ayin and pe are correct and in this poem's standard order, which must not be read as the reversed order of the poems that follow; mark disclosure is complete and correctly typed; the paseq counts (one at Lam.1.15, two at Lam.1.16) match the inventory exactly; the spliced refrain re-collates at byte tier; the translation renderings are verbatim.

items.claim: The span's byte claims all verify - the suffix shift on the third refrain site, the closing letter, the distinct closing mark, the ketiv/qere disclosure and the address structure that justifies not splitting the final verse.
items.evidence: The refrain at the third site is אֵ֤ין מְנַחֵם֙ לִ֔י (oshb:Lam.1.21, byte tier; there is no one to comfort me), which re-collates at byte tier and carries the first-person-singular suffix, against the third-person feminine suffix at the two earlier sites (sweep: 3 verses for the contiguous two-token form: Lam.1.9, Lam.1.17, Lam.1.21) - the shift the reading claims is exactly what the bytes show. Letters tsadi, qof, resh, shin and tav close the poem's letter run; the mark layer is SAMEKH at the front-seam neighbour and the four interior verses and PE at the closing verse, single-witness and never conflated. The ketiv/qere note at Lam.1.18 is disclosed, which is load-bearing because the note sits on the very word rendered 'peoples' in the appeal the reading cites. The address structure is byte-visible and supports the rejected split: שִׁמְעוּ נָ֣א (oshb:Lam.1.18, byte tier) is a second-person plural imperative addressed to the peoples, while Lam.1.20-Lam.1.22 address the deity in the second-person masculine singular - אַתָּ֖ה עָשִׂ֑יתָ (oshb:Lam.1.21, byte tier) and עוֹלַ֛לְתָּ (oshb:Lam.1.22, byte tier) - so the closing imprecation does sit inside a sustained second-person address to the deity and cutting it out would be an over-fine split. All five translation renderings are verbatim. One imprecision worth recording rather than challenging: the span opens on an appeal to the peoples, not to the deity, so the phrase 'one sustained address' describes Lam.1.20-Lam.1.22 rather than the whole span.

items.claim: Every disclosure digit in this reading verifies, but its back seam is drawn on exactly the topic-only ground the reading rejects for an internal split, with the third-person report and one of its own cited formulas running across that seam undisclosed.
items.evidence: The reading rejects an internal split partway through the span because no voice or addressee change marks that line, only a change of topic - and then draws its own closing seam on the same kind of ground. A complete scan of Lam.2.1 through Lam.2.12 returns no second-person form and no first-person-singular form, so no person change occurs anywhere at the back edge; the nearest byte-marked voice change is the first-person onset at Lam.2.11, עֵינַי֙ (oshb:Lam.2.11, byte tier), one verse past the seam. The daughter-of-Zion formula, one of the reading's own cited signals, stands at בַּת צִיּ֔וֹן (oshb:Lam.2.8, byte tier) and again at בַת צִיּ֔וֹן (oshb:Lam.2.10, byte tier), straddling the seam undisclosed (sweep: 8 verses book-wide for the two-token phrase). The remaining material cited for the edge is the mark layer, which is present at every verse of this poem and therefore cannot discriminate one cut from another, and is in any case weak single-witness corroboration rather than a driver. What holds, and holds exactly: the opening cry אֵיכָה֩ (oshb:Lam.2.1, byte tier) is verse-initial (sweep: 3 verses book-wide, verse-initial only); the formula בַּת צִיּ֔וֹן (oshb:Lam.2.1, byte tier) re-collates at byte tier; letters alef through tet are correct; the mark disclosure is complete, with the closing PE of the previous poem named as the front-seam neighbour and never conflated with SAMEKH; the paseq census - one segment apiece at Lam.2.1, Lam.2.5, Lam.2.6, Lam.2.7 and Lam.2.8 - matches the inventory verse for verse; the ketiv/qere note at Lam.2.2 is disclosed; the note that this poem's later letters run in the reversed order is correct and correctly confined to verses outside the span; and the two divine titles are kept apart: אֲדֹנָי֙ (oshb:Lam.2.1, byte tier) stands in 4 verses of the span (sweep: 4 verses: Lam.2.1, Lam.2.2, Lam.2.5, Lam.2.7) and יְהוָ֤ה (oshb:Lam.2.6, byte tier) in 4 (sweep: 4 verses: Lam.2.6, Lam.2.7, Lam.2.8, Lam.2.9) - each digit naming its Hebrew object, not an English rendering - and the rendering quoted at the opening verse matches the title actually standing there.

items.claim: One cited digit is attached to the wrong swept object, and the second-person address the reading names as its strongest closing seam continues unbroken across that seam, undisclosed.
items.evidence: First, the digit. The three-token phrase בְּתוּלַ֖ת בַּת צִיּ֑וֹן (oshb:Lam.2.13, byte tier) stands in exactly 1 verse book-wide (sweep: 1 verse), not 2; the figure of 2 belongs to the shorter two-token pattern, whose other site is לִבְתוּלַ֖ת בַּת יְהוּדָֽה (oshb:Lam.1.15, byte tier) - a different daughter-name, and there behind a single prefix letter, the one prefix the per-length test tolerates at that site. Object and digit do not match, and this is precisely the two-token phrase-test trap these formulas carry. Second, the seam. The second-person feminine-singular address opened in Lam.2.13 - אֲעִידֵ֞ךְ and וַאֲנַֽחֲמֵ֔ךְ (oshb:Lam.2.13, byte tier) - continues without a break into Lam.2.14 with נְבִיאַ֗יִךְ חָ֤זוּ לָךְ֙ (oshb:Lam.2.14, byte tier) and עֲוֺנֵ֖ךְ (oshb:Lam.2.14, byte tier; this verse carries a ketiv/qere note, disclosed here because forms are spliced from it), and on to Lam.2.19. A complete enumeration of every token in this poem ending in final kaf shows second-person feminine-singular forms in exactly 7 consecutive verses, Lam.2.13 through Lam.2.19, and in no other verse of the poem (sweep: 7 verses); the verses after that chain turn to a second-person masculine-singular address to the deity, הָרַ֨גְתָּ֙ בְּי֣וֹם אַפֶּ֔ךָ (oshb:Lam.2.21, byte tier), a different addressee. So the closing seam cuts the address chain at its first joint, and the reading treats the address as the seam rather than as the feature that argues continuity across it. Third, the same seam is straddled by a formula the reading itself counts: daughter-of-Jerusalem stands at הַבַּת֙ יְר֣וּשָׁלִַ֔ם (oshb:Lam.2.13, byte tier) and בַּ֖ת יְרוּשָׁלִָ֑ם (oshb:Lam.2.15, byte tier), one site on each side (sweep: 2 verses book-wide) - correct as a digit, undisclosed as a straddle. Fourth, the unit label names direct address for a span in which only the final verse carries any second-person form at all: the first three verses run third-person plural, then first-person singular, then third-person plural, with no disclosure of the deviation. What holds: בַּת עַמִּ֑י (oshb:Lam.2.11, byte tier) re-collates at byte tier and its census of 5 verses book-wide is exact; all three splices reach byte tier; the letters yod, kaf, lamed and mem are correct; mark disclosure is complete from the front-seam neighbour; the span carries no paseq and no ketiv/qere note and none is claimed; the translation renderings are verbatim.

items.claim: The reading's sole boundary ground - that the address to the personified city gives way at the span's first verse to a third-person report - is inverted relative to the pointed text: all four verses of the span address the city in the second-person feminine singular.
items.evidence: Every verse of the span carries second-person feminine-singular addressee marking: נְבִיאַ֗יִךְ חָ֤זוּ לָךְ֙ (oshb:Lam.2.14, byte tier) and עֲוֺנֵ֖ךְ (oshb:Lam.2.14, byte tier; this verse carries a ketiv/qere note, disclosed because forms are spliced from it); סָֽפְק֨וּ עָלַ֤יִךְ (oshb:Lam.2.15, byte tier); עָלַ֤יִךְ פִּיהֶם֙ כָּל א֣וֹיְבַ֔יִךְ (oshb:Lam.2.16, byte tier); עָלַ֨יִךְ֙ אוֹיֵ֔ב and קֶ֥רֶן צָרָֽיִךְ (oshb:Lam.2.17, byte tier). A complete enumeration of every token in this poem ending in final kaf returns second-person feminine-singular forms in exactly 7 consecutive verses, Lam.2.13 through Lam.2.19, and in no other verse of the poem (sweep: 7 verses) - the span sits wholly inside that chain. What actually changes at the front seam is the speaker's self-reference, not the addressee: the first-person verbs of the preceding verse, אֲעִידֵ֞ךְ and וַאֲנַֽחֲמֵ֔ךְ (oshb:Lam.2.13, byte tier), drop out, while the addressee marking is unchanged. The finite verbs of the following three verses are indeed third-person, but a third-person verb with a second-person addressee is not a third-person report, and the rejected alternative rests on the same inverted contrast. Consequences: the unit label, which names third-person description of the city, and the third-person-narrator signal key are both unsupported at every verse of the span. Both seams cut the same chain and neither is disclosed: at the front, the daughter-of-Jerusalem formula stands on both sides (oshb:Lam.2.13 and oshb:Lam.2.15, sweep: 2 verses book-wide); at the back, the address runs straight on into בַּת עֵינֵֽךְ (oshb:Lam.2.18, byte tier) and כַּפַּ֗יִךְ (oshb:Lam.2.19, byte tier), and the second-person imperatives there are the chain's continuation, not a fresh start. The reading also contains no Hebrew run at all, so a person claim about the source text is made with no quoted byte evidence. What holds and should be preserved in any repair: the letter disclosure - nun, samekh, pe, ayin - is byte-correct, and naming the pe-before-ayin order as a fact of this witness rather than an error to be corrected is exactly right; mark disclosure is complete and correctly typed from the front-seam neighbour; the ketiv/qere note at Lam.2.14 is disclosed; the quoted taunt in the third verse is correctly read as the enemies' own words rather than a communal voice; the translation renderings are verbatim.
